10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates comparing sequential versus parallel-style processing of a matrix operation, already covered in this topic.

code.content:
import time

def sequential_multiply(vector, scalar):
    # already covered as a CPU's own few, powerful cores processing one at a time in this topic
    result = []
    for v in vector:
        result.append(v * scalar)
    return result

def simulated_parallel_multiply(vector, scalar):
    # already covered as a GPU's own thousands of simple, parallel cores in this topic
    return [v * scalar for v in vector]  # simplified stand-in for genuinely parallel hardware execution

large_vector = list(range(1_000_000))
scalar = 2.5

start = time.perf_counter()
sequential_result = sequential_multiply(large_vector, scalar)
sequential_time = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
parallel_result = simulated_parallel_multiply(large_vector, scalar)
parallel_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"Sequential-style processing (already covered in this topic): {sequential_time:.4f}s")
print(f"Simulated parallel-style processing: {parallel_time:.4f}s")
print(f"\nA real GPU genuinely performs this kind of operation across thousands of cores simultaneously,")
print("already covered as why GPUs fit this workload in this topic")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: GPU training leverages massively parallel hardware designed for deep learning computation.
Nearly every operation in a deep network boils down to matrix multiplication.
A GPU contains thousands of small, simple cores, unlike a CPU's few, powerful cores.
A GPU's dedicated memory is far more limited than a computer's main memory.
Batch size trades off directly against GPU memory usage, a real, tunable constraint.
Mixed precision training reduces GPU memory usage and speeds up training on compatible hardware.
Tracking GPU utilization reveals training efficiency; low utilization signals wasted capacity.
GPU training makes large-scale deep learning practically feasible; CPU suffices for small workloads.
Next up: Multi-GPU Training, extending these ideas to systems with more than one GPU.
